Every place is a set of hexes. Each hex carries its share of built-up land, trees, shrubs, grass, cropland, bare ground, water and wetland, plus its population, elevation and a flood screening value. The levers change the cover of specific hexes, and five scores are computed from the new map. Scores run from {0} to {1} and compare scenarios within one place. The weights are modelling choices made so that the levers trade off against each other. They are not forecasts.

A hex counts as built up when a quarter or more of it is buildings and paving. Built-up hexes split into dense core, mid-density and sprawl edge by population per km². Green hexes surrounded by city on three or more sides become city parks. Where none exist, new park sites go in the densest districts.

Each built-up hex gets a heat load, set three quarters by how much of it is paved or roofed and one quarter by population density. Street trees lower it, and so do cool neighbors such as forest, wetland, water, parks, greenways and farmland. Compact growth raises density because the same people live on less land.

A hex is flood-prone when a river runs through it, or when it sits within about {0} km of a river, lake or sea and less than {1} m above it. Rivers come from OpenStreetMap, because satellites miss narrow ones. Canals and small streams are drawn on the map but are not treated as flood sources, since most are controlled channels. People living in flood-prone built-up hexes carry the exposure. Restored wetlands hold the most water, with street trees and regenerative soils adding a little.

Forest, wetland, open grassland, water, parks, corridors and regenerative farms count as habitat. The score blends how much habitat exists, how much of it sits in one connected network, and how many city parks join that network. Corridors follow the cheapest path from the largest natural area to each park, avoiding dense districts where they can.

Cropland in the region is compared with what its people would need at about {0} hectares each, roughly the world average. Regenerative farms yield slightly less in a normal year and hold up much better in a drought. Farms near restored wetlands keep more water in a dry year.

Each action gets its own ranking on today's map. Street trees go first where heat load and population are highest. Wetlands go first on low floodplain land with the most people in flood-prone homes within two hex rings. Corridors start with parks that are cut off from the main habitat, favoring short links near many people. Regenerative farming starts on farmland in the floodplain or next to habitat. Compact growth starts with the outermost sprawl, sooner where it floods. Sites that touch a site already listed are skipped, so each list covers more ground.

The Explore page turns each plan into rough sizes, costs and yearly benefits: street trees counted at up to about {0} per km² of built-up land, and hectares of new wetland, corridor and regenerative farmland counted from the hexes that change. Unit costs and benefits come from published US studies, listed with links under “Sources and assumptions” on the Explore page. They are order-of-magnitude figures for comparing plans, scaled to each country’s price level with World Bank data and shown in US dollars.
Rises as sprawl is pulled back, with a small bonus for greenways and shade that make walking easier.

Levers cost different amounts per point: shade {0}, corridors {1}, wetlands {2}, regenerative farming {3} and compact growth {4}, against a cap of {5}. The best-mix search tries every combination in steps of {6} that fits the cap. Several quite different mixes often score within a point or two of the best, so there is usually more than one good route.

By {0} nearly {1} in {2} people are expected to live in cities. That future is already on its way. What is still open is whether those cities can stand up to the heat, floods and droughts that will come with it.

Every city is tied to the land around it. Rivers and aquifers bring its water. Farmland feeds it. Forests and wetlands cool its air, soak up its floods and shelter the wildlife it shares. Most people living in a city never see these threads, and most plans stop at the city limits.

If you plan cities, manage land or work on climate, you have seen what happens when a city is planned as if it stood alone. The work now is to make cities behave more like living systems, with more green, more water held in place and more room for wildlife, and to plan them together with the land that keeps them alive. It is urgent, and Threadlands is built to help.
